title: test-0122-SOC-GEO-SOILS
passage: Soil formation is a complex process influenced by climate, parent rock, and relief. Alluvial soil, the most widespread type, is not restricted to the Northern Plains; it is also found in the eastern coastal plains, particularly in the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri rivers. Alluvial soil is categorized into two types based on age: Khadar and Bangar. Khadar is the new alluvium, which is more fertile due to its fine texture and frequent renewal by floods, whereas Bangar contains higher concentrations of kanker nodules and is less fertile. Another significant type is black soil, often called Regur soil. Its dark color is primarily due to its composition of clayey material and metallic oxides, rather than high humus content. While soil is a natural resource, it faces degradation. Soil erosion is the removal of topsoil, caused not only by human actions like deforestation and overgrazing but also by natural forces like wind and flowing water. To protect our land, we must adopt conservation methods such as contour ploughing, terrace farming, and shelter belts to reduce the speed of water and wind, ensuring the long-term productivity of our agricultural fields.
